'''trigloid''' (trig′loid), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< ''Trigla'' + ''-oi'' '''I.''' ''a.'' Resembling or related to the gurnar belonging to the ''Triglidæ'' in a broad sense; or pertaining to the ''Trigloidea''. ''Proc. U. S. N'' ''Museum'', XI. 588.

'''II.''' ''n.'' A gurnard or related fish; any me ber of the ''Trigloidea''.

'''Trigloidea''' (trig-loi′dẹ̄-ä), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Tri'' + Gr. εἶδος, form.] A superfamily of acanth terygian fishes, represented by the ''Triglidæ'' related families. {{smaller|The post-temporal forms an inte part of the cranium; the posterotemporal is contigu to the proscapula; and the third suborbital is greatly larged and covers the cheek, articulating behind with anterior wall of the preoperculum.}}

'''triglot''' (trī′glot), ''a.'' [< Gr. τρεῖς (τρι-), three γλῶσσα, γλῶττα, tongue.] Containing, compo in, or relating to three languages: as, a ''tri'' dictionary.

'''trigly''' (trig′li), ''adv.'' [< ''trig''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.] In a manner; neatly; trimly; finely. [Provin or colloq.]

{{smaller block|So he that hathe a consciens cleere
May stand to hys takkell ''tryklye''.
{{right|''Elderton'', Lenten Stuffe (1570). (''Halliw''}}}}

{{smaller block|O busk yir locks ''trigly'', an' kilt up yir coaties.
{{right|''Tarras'', Poems, p. 124. (''Jamies''}}}}

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|trigloid|6477|trigonocerous}}</noinclude>'''trigloid''' (trig′loid), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< ''Trigla'' + ''-oi'' '''I.''' ''a.'' Resembling or related to the gurnar belonging to the ''Triglidæ'' in a broad sense; or pertaining to the ''Trigloidea''. ''Proc. U. S. N'' ''Museum'', XI. 588.

'''II.''' ''n.'' A gurnard or related fish; any me ber of the ''Trigloidea''.

'''Trigloidea''' (trig-loi′dẹ̄-ä), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Tri'' + Gr. εἶδος, form.] A superfamily of acanth terygian fishes, represented by the ''Triglidæ'' related families. {{smaller|The post-temporal forms an inte part of the cranium; the posterotemporal is contigu to the proscapula; and the third suborbital is greatly larged and covers the cheek, articulating behind with anterior wall of the preoperculum.}}

'''triglot''' (trī′glot), ''a.'' [< Gr. τρεῖς (τρι-), three γλῶσσα, γλῶττα, tongue.] Containing, compo in, or relating to three languages: as, a ''tri'' dictionary.

'''trigly''' (trig′li), ''adv.'' [< ''trig''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.] In a manner; neatly; trimly; finely. [Provin or colloq.]

{{smaller block|So he that hathe a consciens cleere
May stand to hys takkell ''tryklye''.
{{right|''Elderton'', Lenten Stuffe (1570). (''Halliw''}}}}

{{smaller block|O busk yir locks ''trigly'', an' kilt up yir coaties.
{{right|''Tarras'', Poems, p. 124. (''Jamies''}}}}

'''triglyceride''' (trī-glis′e-rid or -rīd), ''n.'' [< τρεῖς (τρι-), three, + E. ''glycer-in'' + ''-ide''<sup>1</sup>.] ''chem.'', a substitution product formed by the placement of three hydrogen atoms in glyce by acid radicals. {{smaller|The triglycerides formed by stea palmitic, oleic, and butyric acids make up the larger of most animal and vegetable fats.}}

'''triglyph''' (trī′glif), ''n.'' [= F. ''triglyphe'', < L. ''glyphus'', < Gr. τρίγλυφος, a three-grooved bl in the Doric frieze, prop. adj., three-groove τρεῖς (τρι-), three, + γλύφειν, carve, groove, γλ a cutting, a channel: see ''glyph''.] In ''arch'' structural member in the frieze of the D order, repeated at equal intervals, usually o every column and over the middle of every tercolumniation. {{smaller|The typical Greek triglyph is a sive block incised with two entire vertical grooves to a right angle, called ''glyphs'', framed between three lets, and with a semi-groove at each side. The bloc grooved on both sides to receive the adjoining meto which are thin slabs slid into their places from above. triglyphs represent the ends of the ceiling-beams of primitive wooden construction. In Greek use the terior triglyphs of a range are always slightly displa so as to occupy the angles of the frieze instead of com like the others, over the centers of the columns; in man and affiliated architectures this refinement does occur; and in Roman and even some of the later Greek amples the triglyphs are merely carved in relief in face of the frieze-blocks, instead of being, as properly dependent blocks. See also cuts under ''entablature'' ''monotriglyph.''}}

[[File:century v08 p0281 c1f1.png|center|360px]]
{{c|A Triglyph of the Parthenon, showing the groove in one side o block into which the metope was slid.}}

{{smaller block|All round between the ''triglyphs'' in the frieze there most exquisite alt-reliefs of combats with centaurs, li and many on horses.
{{right|''Pococke'', Description of the East, II. ii.}}}}

¶
'''triglyphal''' (trī′glif-al), ''a.'' [< ''triglyph'' + - Same as ''triglyphic. Amer. Jour. Archæol.'', VI.

'''triglyphic''' (trī-glif′ik), ''a.'' [< ''triglyph'' + - 1. Consisting of or pertaining to triglyphs 2. Containing three sets of characters or scu tures.

'''triglyphical''' (trī-glif′i-ka̤l), ''a.'' [< ''triglyphic'' -''al.''] Same as ''triglyphic.''

'''trigness''' (trig′nes), ''n.'' The state of being t or trim; neatness. [Provincial or colloq.]

{{smaller block|The lassies who had been at Nanse Bank's sc were always well spoken of . . . for the ''trigness'' of t houses, when they were afterwards married.
{{right|''Galt'', Annals of the Parish, p.}}}}

'''trigon<sup>1</sup>''' (trī′gon), ''n.'' [< F. ''trigone'' = Sp. ''gono'', also ''trigon'' = Pg. It. ''trigono'', < L. ''tri'' ''num'', also ''trigonium'', < Gr. τρίγωνον, a triangle musical instrument so called, neut. of τρίγω three-cornered, triangled, < τρεῖς (τρι-), three γωνία, angle.] 1. A triangle. {{smaller block|As when the cranes direct their flight on high,
To cut their way, they in a ''trigon'' flie;
Which pointed figure may with ease diuide
Opposing blasts, through which they swiftly glide.
{{right|''Sir J. Beaumont'', Bosworth Field.}}}}
2. In ''astrol.'': (''a'') The junction of three signs, the zodiac being divided into four trigons: the ''watery trigon'', which includes Cancer, Scorpio, and Pisces; the ''earthly trigon'', Taurus, Virgo, and Capricornus; the ''airy trigon'', Gemini, Libra, and Aquarius; and the ''fiery trigon'', Aries, Leo, and Sagittarius.

{{smaller block|Look [in the almanac] whether the ''fiery Trigon'', his man, be not lisping to his master's old tables, his note-book, his counsel-keeper.
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., ii. 4. 288.}}}}
(''b'') Trine: an aspect of two planets distant 120 degrees from each other.—3. In ''antiq.'': (''a'') A kind of triangular lyre or harp. Also called ''trigonon.'' (''b'') A game at ball played by three persons standing so as to be at the angles of a triangle.—4. An instrument of a triangular form, used in dialing. ''Kersey'', 1708.—5. In ''conch.'', a shell of the genus ''Trigonia.''

'''trigon'''<sup>2</sup>† (trig′on), ''n.'' [Also ''trigen''; appar. for *''triggin'', a dial. form of *''trigging'', < ''trig''<sup>3</sup> + ''-ing''<sup>1</sup>.] A trig; a skid.

{{smaller block|And stoppeth the wheel with a ''Trigen'' [Sufflamine] in a steep descent.
{{right|''Hoole'', tr. of The Visible World, lxxxvi.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Trigon'', a Pole to stop the Wheel of a Cart, where it goes too fast down a steep Place.
{{right|''Bailey'', 1731.}}}}

'''trigonal''' (trig′ọ̄-nal), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< ''trigon''<sup>1</sup> + ''-al.''] I. ''a.'' 1. Pertaining to a trigon; having the form of a trigon; triangular.—2. In ''entom.'', triangular in cross-section; having three long edges; trihedral; prismatic: as, ''trigonal'' antennæ; ''trigonal'' joints.—3. In ''bot.'', same as ''trigonous''.—4. In ''anat.'', noting a triangular space at the base of the bladder. See ''trigonum'' (''a''). {{smaller|—'''Trigonal coördinate,''' one of a set of three coördinates of a point in a plane, which are related to trilinear coördinates as follows. Let <math>x_{n+1} = y_n/z_n</math>, <math>y_{n+1} = z_n/x_n</math>, <math>z_{n+1} = x_n/y_n</math>, and let <math>x_0</math>, <math>y_0</math>, <math>z_0</math> be trilinear coördinates. Then <math>x_n</math>, <math>y_n</math>, <math>z_n</math> are called trigonal coördinates of the ''n''th class. Trigonal coördinates are subject to the equation <math>x_n y_n z_n = 1</math>, which does not vary with the triangle of reference. They are valuable for studying higher plane curves. Thus, a linear equation in trigonal coördinates of the first class represents a cubic. They were invented by S. Levi in 1876, and must not be confounded with Walton's trigonic coördinates.—'''Trigonal residue.''' See ''residue''.—'''Trigonal trapezohedron.''' See ''tetartohedrism''.—'''Trigonal trisoctahedron.''' See ''trisoctahedron''.}}

II. ''n.'' In ''anat.'', the triangular space at the base of the bladder; the trigonum.

'''Trigonalidæ''' (trig-ọ̄-nal′i-dē), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Trigonalys'' + ''-idæ''.] A family of parasitic hymenopters, having the single genus ''Trigonalys''.

'''trigonally''' (trig′ọ̄-nal-i), ''adv.'' Triangularly.

'''Trigonalys''' (trī-gon′a̤-lis), ''n.'' [NL. (Westwood, 1835), < Gr. τρίγωνος, three-cornered, + (irreg.) ἅλως, a threshing-floor, a disk: see ''halo''.] An anomalous genus of hymenopterous insects, formerly placed in the family ''Evaniidæ'', now considered as forming a family by itself. {{smaller|The abdomen is attached to the extremity of the thorax, the fore wings have two recurrent nervures, and the first submarginal and first discoidal cells are distinct. Three}} European and four North American species are known.

'''trigonate''' (trig′ọ̄-nāt), ''a.'' [< ''trigon''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ate''<sup>1</sup>.] In ''entom.'', same as ''trigonal'', 2.

'''trigone''' (trī′gōn), ''n.'' [= F. ''trigone'', < NL. ''trigonum'', < Gr. τρίγωνος, three-cornered.] The trigonum of the bladder. See ''trigonum'' (''a'').

'''Trigonella''' (trig-ō-nel′ä), ''n.'' [NL. (Linnæus, 1737), so called with ref. to the three-cornered appearance of the flower; < Gr. τρίγωνος, three-cornered (see ''trigon''<sup>1</sup>), + dim. ''-ella''.] A genus of leguminous plants, of the tribe ''Trifolieæ'', characterized by obtuse keel-petals, numerous ovules, and a pod which is straight, falcate, or arcuate, but not spiral.
{{smaller block|There are about 60 species, natives of Europe, Asia, and North Africa, with a few in South Africa, and one, ''T. suavissima'', in the interior of Australia. They are usually strong-smelling herbs, having pinnately trifoliate leaves with adnate stipules. Most of the species bear yellow or white flowers in a head or short raceme. The pod is linear, its veins being reticulated in the section ''Buceras''; in ''Falcatula'' it is broad and compressed, and its veins are straight. In a few similar species, the section ''Pocockia'', the pod bears winged or fringed sutures. In three smaller sections with beaked pods, the flowers in ''Uncinella'' are usually pendulous, in ''Fænum-græcum'' solitary, in ''Grammocarpus'' blue. Several of the species, especially ''T. Fænum-græcum'', are known as ''fenugreek'' (which see). ''T. cærulea'' is the Swiss melilot. ''T. ornithopodioides'' is the bird's-foot fenugreek, a reddish-flowered prostrate species growing on British heaths. ''T. ornithorhynchus'' is the bird's-bill fenugreek, a yellow Russian species with fleshy leaves, spiny peduncles, and pods with a recurving beak. ''T. suavissima'' has been found valuable for pasturage in Australia.}}

[[File:century v08 p0281 c2f1.png|center|138px]]
{{c|Plant with Flowers and Fruits of Fenugreek (''Trigonella Fænum-græcum''). ''a'', a fruit.}}

'''trigonellite''' (trig-ọ̄-nel′īt), ''n.'' [As ''Trigonella'' + ''-ite''<sup>2</sup>.] A fossil shelly substance. See ''aptychus.''

'''trigoneutic''' (trī-gọ̄-nū′tik), ''a.'' [< Gr. τρεῖς (τρι-), three, + γονεύειν, beget.] In ''entom.'', triple-brooded; having three broods in a single year. See ''trivoltine.''

'''trigoneutism''' (trī-gọ̄-nū′tizm), ''n.'' [< ''trigoneut(ic)'' + ''-ism.''] The state or character of being trigoneutic or triple-brooded.

[[File:century v08 p0281 c3f1.png|center|149px]]
{{c|A Trigon (''Trigonia costata'').}}

'''Trigonia''' (trī-gō′ni-ä̤), ''n'' 1791), < Gr. τρίγωνος, three-cornered: see ''trigon''<sup>1</sup>.] 1. The typical genus of the family ''Trigoniidæ''. ''T. margaritacea'' is the pearly trigon. See also cut under ''Trigoniidæ''.—2. [''l. c.''] A shell of the genus ''Trigonia'' or family ''Trigoniidæ;'' a trigon: also used attributively: as, the ''trigonia'' beds or grits.—{{smaller|'''Trigonia beds''', a subdivision of the Corallian division of the Jurassic, especially well developed at Osmington near Weymouth, England.—'''Trigonia grits''', subdivisions of the Oölite in England. The Upper and Lower Trigonia grits are subdivisions of the Upper and Lower Ragstones, which are themselves divisions of the Inferior Oölite in Gloucestershire.}}

'''Trigoniacea''' (trī-gō-ni-ā′sẹ̄-ä), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Trigonia'' + ''-acea''.] A superfamily of integripalliate isomyarian bivalve mollusks, represented by the family ''Trigoniidæ''.

'''trigoniacean''' (tri-gō-ni-ā′sẹ̄-a̤n), ''a.'' and ''n.'' '''I.''' ''a.'' Of or pertaining to the ''Trigoniacea''.

'''II.''' ''n.'' A member of the ''Trigoniacea''.

'''trigonic''' (trī-gon′ik), ''a.'' [< ''trigon''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ic''.] Pertaining to a trigon or triangle.—{{smaller|'''Trigonic coördinate''', one of a set of three coördinates determining the position of a point in a plane, these being the three angles subtended between three points of reference as seen from the point whose position is in question: invented by William Walton in 1868, and not to be confounded with trilinear or with trigonal coördinates.}}

'''Trigoniidæ''' (trig-ọ̄-nī′i-dē), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Trigonia'' + ''-idæ''.] A family of dimyarian bivalves. The mantle-margins are free and without siphons; the branchiæ are ample and unequal; the foot is long and angulated behind; the palpi are small and pointed; the shell is equivalve and nacreous within; the umbones are antemedian; the ligament is external; the cardinal teeth are divergent, and more or less transversely striated; and the pallial impression is entire. It is a group of mollusks whose living species are few and con{{smaller|fined to the Australian seas, but which had an extensive range from the Triassic to the Cretaceous epoch. The typical genus is ''Trigonia''. Also ''Trigoniadæ'', ''Trigonidæ''. See also cut under ''Trigonia''.}}

[[File:century v08 p0281 c3f2.png|center|163px]]
{{c|Structure of ''Trigoniidæ'' (''Trigonia pectinata''). ''a'', ''a''′, adductors; ''f'', foot; ''hl'', hinge-ligament; ''lt'', labial tentacles or palpi; ''m'', margin; ''o'', mouth; ''p'', pallial line; ''t'', ''t''′, dental sockets; ''v'', cloaca.}}

¶
'''Trigonocarpus''' (trig″ọ̄-nọ̄-kär′pus), ''n.'' [NL., < Gr. τρίγωνος, three-cornered, + καρπός, fruit.] The generic name given by Brongniart (1828) to certain fossil fruits, very abundant in the coal-measures of both the Old World and the New World, the botanical relations of which are still uncertain. {{smaller|These fruits are ovoid in shape, with either three or six strongly marked ribs, which are more distinct toward the base, and sometimes disappear above; at the apex is a small round or triangular cavity.}}

'''trigonocephalous''' (trig″ọ̄-nō-sef′a̤-lus), ''a.'' [< Gr. τρίγωνος, three-cornered, + κεφαλή, head.] Having a flattened and somewhat triangular head, as a venomous serpent of the genus ''Trigonocephalus''.

'''Trigonocephalus''' (trig″ọ̄-nọ̄-sef′a̤-lus), ''n.'' [NL. (Oppel, 1811), < Gr. τρίγωνος, three-cornered, + κεφαλή, head.] A genus of venomous serpents, of the family ''Crotalidæ'': used with various applications. See ''Ancistrodon'', ''Craspedocephalus'', ''Toxicophis'', ''copperhead'', ''fer-de-lance'', and ''moccasin''<sup>2</sup>.

'''trigonocerous''' (trig-ō-nos′e-rus), ''a.'' [< Gr. τρίγωνος, three-cornered, + κέρας, horn.] Having horns with three angles, edges, or ridges—that is, triangular in cross-section.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
